newsitem.title: RUSSIA: No output halts at Russian nickel,aluminium plants.
newsitem.headline: No output halts at Russian nickel,aluminium plants.

text.p: Protests and strikes across Russia on Thursday did not affect production at nickel and aluminium plants, although some workers in auxiliary jobs at some metals firms joined demonstrations, officials said.

"The workers of our plant have decided not to take part in strikes," said an official at the Sayansk Aluminium smelter who declined to be named. "Wages are being paid normally and very few people are expected to participate in protests."
He said there were no disruptions to output or exports at Russia's third largest primary aluminium smelter.

Anatoly Komrakov, spokesman for the Norilsk Nickel metals group, said no workers connected to mining, refining or exports had struck, but some employees in auxiliary jobs at the flagship plant had joined protests.
"Under the agreement reached, there will be no actions directed at interfering with mining, output or exports in the period to July 1," he said.

Norilsk said on Tuesday that the trade union strike committee at the flagship combine had agreed not to disrupt production or loading of metals before July 1 and had scrapped plans to disrupt output on Thursday and from April 2.
Komrakov said 800-1,000 auxiliary workers had gathered outside the main plant's administrative building to wave red Soviet flags and call for a return to socialism.
The main plant, a key world producer of nickel, cobalt and platinum group metals, has about 120,000 workers.
A spokesman at the Bratsk aluminium smelter, the world's largest, said there were no disruptions.
"There are no disruptions, everyone is working normally," said Luiza Zhuravlyova from the Siberian city of Bratsk.

Hundreds of thousands of citizens across Russia participated in protest marches over wage and pension arrears, waving red banners and calling for a return to the past. Some exhorted President Boris Yeltsin and his new reformist cabinet to resign.
The turnout appeared to be far below national union leaders' predictions that 20 million protestors would participate. --Andrei Khalip, Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941 8520
